sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: Use the ratio test to determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n}{2^n}$ converges.
questions.answer: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{n+1}{2n} = \frac{1}{2} < 1$: converges.
questions.explanation: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{n+1}{2n} = \frac{1}{2} < 1$: converges.

questions.q: Use the ratio test on $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n!}{n^n}$.
questions.answer: $\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \frac{n^n}{(n+1)^n} = \left(\frac{n}{n+1}\right)^n \rightarrow \frac{1}{e} < 1$: converges.
questions.explanation: $\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \frac{n^n}{(n+1)^n} = \left(\frac{n}{n+1}\right)^n \rightarrow \frac{1}{e} < 1$: converges.

questions.q: Use the comparison test to determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2+3}$ converges, by comparing to $\sum \frac{1}{n^2}$.
questions.answer: $0 < \frac{1}{n^2+3} < \frac{1}{n^2}$ for all $n \geq 1$, and $\sum\frac{1}{n^2}$ is a convergent $p$-series ($p=2>1$), so by comparison the given series converges.
questions.explanation: $0 < \frac{1}{n^2+3} < \frac{1}{n^2}$ for all $n \geq 1$, and $\sum\frac{1}{n^2}$ is a convergent $p$-series ($p=2>1$), so by comparison the given series converges.

questions.q: Determine whether each $p$-series converges or diverges:
questions.target: Alternating series and the p-series test
questions.answer: (a) Converges ($p=3>1$).; (b) Diverges ($p=\frac{1}{2}\leq 1$).
questions.explanation: (a) Converges ($p=3>1$).; (b) Diverges ($p=\frac{1}{2}\leq 1$).

questions.q: Determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$ converges, and classify it as absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent, or divergent.
questions.target: Alternating series and the p-series test
questions.answer: The terms $\frac{1}{n}$ decrease to $0$, so by the alternating series test the series converges. But $\sum\frac{1}{n}$ (absolute values) diverges — so the series is conditionally convergent.
questions.explanation: The terms $\frac{1}{n}$ decrease to $0$, so by the alternating series test the series converges. But $\sum\frac{1}{n}$ (absolute values) diverges — so the series is conditionally convergent.

questions.q: Use the integral test to determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n\ln n}$ (starting at $n=2$) converges or diverges, using $\int_2^\infty \frac{1}{x\ln x}\,dx$.
questions.answer: Let $u=\ln x$: $\int\frac{1}{x\ln x}dx = \ln|\ln x|+C$. $\int_2^\infty\frac{dx}{x\ln x} = \lim_{b\rightarrow\infty}\left[\ln(\ln x)\right]_2^b = \infty$: the integral diverges, so by the integral test the series diverges.
questions.explanation: Let $u=\ln x$: $\int\frac{1}{x\ln x}dx = \ln|\ln x|+C$. $\int_2^\infty\frac{dx}{x\ln x} = \lim_{b\rightarrow\infty}\left[\ln(\ln x)\right]_2^b = \infty$: the integral diverges, so by the integral test the series diverges.

questions.q: Use the integral test to confirm that $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2}$ converges, using $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx$.
questions.answer: $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{x^2}dx = \lim_{b\rightarrow\infty}\left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_1^b = 1$, a finite value, so by the integral test the series converges.
questions.explanation: $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{x^2}dx = \lim_{b\rightarrow\infty}\left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_1^b = 1$, a finite value, so by the integral test the series converges.

sections.heading: Part II — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Intermediate Multi-Step Application (8–14)

questions.q: For each series, name the most efficient test to apply (ratio, comparison, $p$-series, or alternating series), without fully evaluating:
answers: Ratio test (factorial in denominator is a strong signal).
questions.answer: (a) Ratio test (factorial in denominator is a strong signal).; (b) Alternating series test (terms decrease to $0$).; (c) $p$-series test directly ($p=4>1$: converges).
questions.explanation: (a) Ratio test (factorial in denominator is a strong signal).; (b) Alternating series test (terms decrease to $0$).; (c) $p$-series test directly ($p=4>1$: converges).

questions.q: Use the limit comparison test to determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n+1}{n^3+2}$ converges, comparing to $\sum\frac{1}{n^2}$.
questions.answer: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{(n+1)/(n^3+2)}{1/n^2} = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{n^3+n^2}{n^3+2} = 1$, a finite positive value. Since $\sum\frac{1}{n^2}$ converges ($p=2>1$), by the limit comparison test the given series also converges.
questions.explanation: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{(n+1)/(n^3+2)}{1/n^2} = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{n^3+n^2}{n^3+2} = 1$, a finite positive value. Since $\sum\frac{1}{n^2}$ converges ($p=2>1$), by the limit comparison test the given series also converges.

questions.q: Use the limit comparison test on $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{3n^2-1}{n^4+2n}$, comparing to $\sum\frac{1}{n^2}$.
questions.answer: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{(3n^2-1)/(n^4+2n)}{1/n^2} = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3n^4-n^2}{n^4+2n} = 3$, finite and positive. Since $\sum\frac{1}{n^2}$ converges, so does the given series.
questions.explanation: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{(3n^2-1)/(n^4+2n)}{1/n^2} = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3n^4-n^2}{n^4+2n} = 3$, finite and positive. Since $\sum\frac{1}{n^2}$ converges, so does the given series.

questions.q: Use the root test to determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{n}{2n+1}\right)^n$ converges.
questions.answer: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sqrt[n]{\left|\left(\frac{n}{2n+1}\right)^n\right|}=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{n}{2n+1}=\frac{1}{2}<1$: converges.
questions.explanation: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sqrt[n]{\left|\left(\frac{n}{2n+1}\right)^n\right|}=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{n}{2n+1}=\frac{1}{2}<1$: converges.

questions.q: Use the root test on $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{3^n}{n^n}$.
questions.answer: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sqrt[n]{\frac{3^n}{n^n}}=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3}{n}=0<1$: converges.
questions.explanation: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sqrt[n]{\frac{3^n}{n^n}}=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3}{n}=0<1$: converges.

questions.q: Determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}$ is absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent, or divergent.
questions.answer: Taking absolute values: $\sum\frac{1}{n^2}$ is a convergent $p$-series ($p=2>1$). Since the series of absolute values converges, the original series is absolutely convergent.
questions.explanation: Taking absolute values: $\sum\frac{1}{n^2}$ is a convergent $p$-series ($p=2>1$). Since the series of absolute values converges, the original series is absolutely convergent.

questions.q: Determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n}{\sqrt{n}}$ is absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent, or divergent.
questions.answer: Absolute values give $\sum\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$, a divergent $p$-series ($p=\frac{1}{2}\leq1$). But the terms $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ decrease to $0$, so by the alternating series test the original series converges. It is conditionally convergent.
questions.explanation: Absolute values give $\sum\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$, a divergent $p$-series ($p=\frac{1}{2}\leq1$). But the terms $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ decrease to $0$, so by the alternating series test the original series converges. It is conditionally convergent.

sections.heading: Part III — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Challenging & Cross-Lesson Synthesis (15–20)

questions.q: The alternating series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^2}$ converges by the alternating series test. Use the fact that the error after $n$ terms is bounded by the first omitted term to estimate how many terms are needed for the partial sum to be within $0.001$ of the true sum.
questions.target: Estimating the sum of an alternating series
questions.answer: Error bound: $|S-S_n|\leq a_{n+1}=\frac{1}{(n+1)^2}$. Need $\frac{1}{(n+1)^2}<0.001$: $(n+1)^2>1000$, so $n+1>31.6$, meaning $n\geq32$ terms suffice.
questions.explanation: Error bound: $|S-S_n|\leq a_{n+1}=\frac{1}{(n+1)^2}$. Need $\frac{1}{(n+1)^2}<0.001$: $(n+1)^2>1000$, so $n+1>31.6$, meaning $n\geq32$ terms suffice.

questions.q: Determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n^2}{3^n}$ converges, using the ratio test.
questions.answer: $\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|=\frac{(n+1)^2}{3^{n+1}}\cdot\frac{3^n}{n^2}=\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{n+1}{n}\right)^2\rightarrow\frac{1}{3}<1$: converges.
questions.explanation: $\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|=\frac{(n+1)^2}{3^{n+1}}\cdot\frac{3^n}{n^2}=\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{n+1}{n}\right)^2\rightarrow\frac{1}{3}<1$: converges.

questions.q: Determine whether $\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n(\ln n)^2}$ converges, using the integral test with $u=\ln x$.
questions.answer: $\int_2^\infty\frac{1}{x(\ln x)^2}\,dx$: with $u=\ln x$, $du=\frac{1}{x}dx$: $\int\frac{1}{u^2}\,du=-\frac{1}{u}+C$. Evaluating: $\lim_{b\rightarrow\infty}\left[-\frac{1}{\ln x}\right]_2^b=0-\left(-\frac{1}{\ln2}\right)=\frac{1}{\ln2}$, a finite value: the integral converges, so by the integral test the series converges.
questions.explanation: $\int_2^\infty\frac{1}{x(\ln x)^2}\,dx$: with $u=\ln x$, $du=\frac{1}{x}dx$: $\int\frac{1}{u^2}\,du=-\frac{1}{u}+C$. Evaluating: $\lim_{b\rightarrow\infty}\left[-\frac{1}{\ln x}\right]_2^b=0-\left(-\frac{1}{\ln2}\right)=\frac{1}{\ln2}$, a finite value: the integral converges, so by the integral test the series converges.

questions.q: A student claims that since $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n}=0$, the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}$ must converge. Explain what is wrong with this reasoning, and state the correct necessary (but not sufficient) condition that the $n$th-term test actually provides, using the harmonic series as a counterexample.
questions.answer: The reasoning confuses a necessary condition with a sufficient one. The $n$th-term test only says: IF $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}a_n\neq0$, THEN the series diverges. It says nothing when the limit IS $0$ — that case is inconclusive. The harmonic series $\sum\frac{1}{n}$ is the standard counterexample: its terms go to $0$, yet the series diverges (proven via the integral test or the comparison/grouping argument), showing that $\lim a_n=0$ alone never guarantees convergence.
questions.explanation: The reasoning confuses a necessary condition with a sufficient one. The $n$th-term test only says: IF $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}a_n\neq0$, THEN the series diverges. It says nothing when the limit IS $0$ — that case is inconclusive. The harmonic series $\sum\frac{1}{n}$ is the standard counterexample: its terms go to $0$, yet the series diverges (proven via the integral test or the comparison/grouping argument), showing that $\lim a_n=0$ alone never guarantees convergence.

questions.q: For the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n^3+2n}{2n^5-n+1}$, first find the $n$th-term limit to check the necessary condition, then use the limit comparison test with $\sum\frac{1}{n^2}$ to determine whether the series converges.
questions.answer: $n$th-term limit: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{n^3+2n}{2n^5-n+1}=0$ (inconclusive by itself). Limit comparison with $\frac{1}{n^2}$: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{(n^3+2n)/(2n^5-n+1)}{1/n^2}=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{n^5+2n^3}{2n^5-n+1}=\frac{1}{2}$, finite and positive. Since $\sum\frac{1}{n^2}$ converges ($p=2>1$), by the limit comparison test the given series also converges.
questions.explanation: $n$th-term limit: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{n^3+2n}{2n^5-n+1}=0$ (inconclusive by itself). Limit comparison with $\frac{1}{n^2}$: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{(n^3+2n)/(2n^5-n+1)}{1/n^2}=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{n^5+2n^3}{2n^5-n+1}=\frac{1}{2}$, finite and positive. Since $\sum\frac{1}{n^2}$ converges ($p=2>1$), by the limit comparison test the given series also converges.

questions.q: A quality-control engineer models cumulative defect probability using $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n\cdot2^n}$. Use the ratio test to confirm this series converges, and briefly explain (in one sentence) why a convergent bound like this is useful for guaranteeing that a manufacturing process's total defect risk stays finite over infinitely many production runs.
questions.answer: $\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|=\frac{n\cdot2^n}{(n+1)\cdot2^{n+1}}=\frac{n}{2(n+1)}\rightarrow\frac{1}{2}<1$: converges. Practically, a convergent bound guarantees the cumulative defect probability approaches a finite ceiling rather than growing without bound as more production runs occur, which is essential for meaningful long-run risk assessment.
questions.explanation: $\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|=\frac{n\cdot2^n}{(n+1)\cdot2^{n+1}}=\frac{n}{2(n+1)}\rightarrow\frac{1}{2}<1$: converges. Practically, a convergent bound guarantees the cumulative defect probability approaches a finite ceiling rather than growing without bound as more production runs occur, which is essential for meaningful long-run risk assessment.

sections.heading: Part IV — Multiple-Choice Questions (MCQs): Foundational Concept Mastery (21–28)

questions.q: For what values of $p$ does the $p$-series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^p}$ converge?
questions.answer: By the Integral Test, $\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx$ converges if and only if $p > 1$. When $p \leq 1$, the $p$-series diverges.
questions.explanation: By the Integral Test, $\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx$ converges if and only if $p > 1$. When $p \leq 1$, the $p$-series diverges.

questions.q: Use the Integral Test to determine the convergence of $\sum_{n=2}^\infty \frac{1}{n\ln n}$.
questions.answer: $\int_2^\infty \frac{1}{x\ln x}\,dx = [\ln(\ln x)]_2^\infty = \infty$. Since the integral diverges, the series diverges.
questions.explanation: $\int_2^\infty \frac{1}{x\ln x}\,dx = [\ln(\ln x)]_2^\infty = \infty$. Since the integral diverges, the series diverges.

questions.q: Which conditions must $f(x)$ satisfy to apply the Integral Test to $\sum a_n$ where $a_n = f(n)$?
choices: $f$ must be continuous, positive, and decreasing on $[1, \infty)$
questions.answer: The Integral Test requires $f(x)$ to be continuous, positive, and eventually decreasing for all $x \geq 1$.
questions.explanation: The Integral Test requires $f(x)$ to be continuous, positive, and eventually decreasing for all $x \geq 1$.

questions.q: Determine the convergence of $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^3 + 5}$.
questions.answer: For $n \geq 1$, $\frac{1}{n^3 + 5} < \frac{1}{n^3}$. Since $\sum 1/n^3$ is a convergent $p$-series ($p = 3 > 1$), the series converges.
questions.explanation: For $n \geq 1$, $\frac{1}{n^3 + 5} < \frac{1}{n^3}$. Since $\sum 1/n^3$ is a convergent $p$-series ($p = 3 > 1$), the series converges.

questions.q: Use the Limit Comparison Test with $b_n = 1/n$ to test $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{2n + 1}{n^2 - 3}$.
questions.answer: $L = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{(2n+1)/(n^2-3)}{1/n} = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{2n^2 + n}{n^2 - 3} = 2$. Since $0 < L < \infty$, both series share the same behavior. Thus it diverges.
questions.explanation: $L = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{(2n+1)/(n^2-3)}{1/n} = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{2n^2 + n}{n^2 - 3} = 2$. Since $0 < L < \infty$, both series share the same behavior. Thus it diverges.

questions.q: Which comparison series $b_n$ is best suited for testing $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\sqrt{n}}{n^2 + 4n}$ via LCT?
questions.answer: The dominant terms are $\frac{\sqrt{n}}{n^2} = \frac{n^{1/2}}{n^2} = \frac{1}{n^{3/2}}$. Since $p = 3/2 > 1$, it is a convergent $p$-series.
questions.explanation: The dominant terms are $\frac{\sqrt{n}}{n^2} = \frac{n^{1/2}}{n^2} = \frac{1}{n^{3/2}}$. Since $p = 3/2 > 1$, it is a convergent $p$-series.

questions.q: What are the two conditions of the Alternating Series Test (AST) for $\sum (-1)^n b_n$ ($b_n > 0$)?
questions.answer: The Leibniz criteria require that the terms are positive, monotonically decreasing ($b_{n+1} \leq b_n$), and have limit 0.
questions.explanation: The Leibniz criteria require that the terms are positive, monotonically decreasing ($b_{n+1} \leq b_n$), and have limit 0.

questions.q: Classify $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$.
questions.answer: The alternating harmonic series converges by AST. However, the series of absolute values $\sum 1/n$ is the divergent harmonic series. Thus it is conditionally convergent.
questions.explanation: The alternating harmonic series converges by AST. However, the series of absolute values $\sum 1/n$ is the divergent harmonic series. Thus it is conditionally convergent.

questions.q: If $S = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^4}$ is approximated by $S_3$, what is the maximum error by the Alternating Series Estimation Theorem?
questions.answer: By the Alternating Series Estimation Theorem, $|R_n| \leq b_{n+1}$. For $n = 3$, $|R_3| \leq b_4 = \frac{1}{4^4} = \frac{1}{256}$.
questions.explanation: By the Alternating Series Estimation Theorem, $|R_n| \leq b_{n+1}$. For $n = 3$, $|R_3| \leq b_4 = \frac{1}{4^4} = \frac{1}{256}$.

questions.q: State the conclusion of the Ratio Test when $L = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| < 1$.
questions.answer: If $L < 1$, the series converges absolutely. If $L > 1$, it diverges. If $L = 1$, the Ratio Test is inconclusive.
questions.explanation: If $L < 1$, the series converges absolutely. If $L > 1$, it diverges. If $L = 1$, the Ratio Test is inconclusive.

questions.q: Apply the Ratio Test to $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{3^n}{n!}$.
questions.answer: $\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \frac{3^{n+1}}{(n+1)!} \frac{n!}{3^n} = \frac{3}{n+1} \rightarrow 0$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$. Since $L = 0 < 1$, the series converges absolutely.
questions.explanation: $\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \frac{3^{n+1}}{(n+1)!} \frac{n!}{3^n} = \frac{3}{n+1} \rightarrow 0$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$. Since $L = 0 < 1$, the series converges absolutely.

questions.q: Use the Root Test to determine the convergence of $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(\frac{2n + 1}{3n - 1}\right)^n$.
questions.answer: $\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \sqrt[n]{|a_n|} = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{2n+1}{3n-1} = \frac{2}{3}$. Since $L = 2/3 < 1$, the series converges absolutely.
questions.explanation: $\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \sqrt[n]{|a_n|} = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{2n+1}{3n-1} = \frac{2}{3}$. Since $L = 2/3 < 1$, the series converges absolutely.

questions.q: By the alternating series estimation theorem, what is the fewest number of terms of $\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$ needed to guarantee an error less than $\frac{1}{10000}$?
questions.answer: The error after summing up to $n=10000$ is at most the next term, $\frac{1}{10001}$ $<$ $\frac{1}{10000}$, while stopping one term earlier leaves a bound $\frac{1}{10000}$ $\geq$ $\frac{1}{10000}$. So 10000 terms are needed.

questions.q: Integral test convergence of $\sum_{n=1}^\infty 1/n(\ln n)^2$ (from $n=2$) gives sum approximately:
questions.target: Estimating the sum of an alternating series
questions.answer: $\int_2^\infty dx/(x(\ln x)^2)=1/\ln2<\infty\Rightarrow$ converges.
questions.explanation: $\int_2^\infty dx/(x(\ln x)^2)=1/\ln2<\infty\Rightarrow$ converges.
questions.cross_lesson: 10.01 Calculus with Parametric and Polar Curves

questions.q: Which test determines $\sum n^2/e^n$? Answer: by ratio test $L=$
questions.answer: $L=\lim(n+1)^2/e^{n+1}\cdot e^n/n^2=1/e<1\Rightarrow$ converges.
questions.explanation: $L=\lim(n+1)^2/e^{n+1}\cdot e^n/n^2=1/e<1\Rightarrow$ converges.

questions.q: Series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty n\cdot(1/2)^n$: ratio test gives $L=$
questions.answer: $|a_{n+1}/a_n|=(n+1)/(2n)\rightarrow1/2<1\Rightarrow$ converges.
questions.explanation: $|a_{n+1}/a_n|=(n+1)/(2n)\rightarrow1/2<1\Rightarrow$ converges.

questions.q: The ratio test for $\sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n/n!$: $|a_{n+1}/a_n|=|x|/(n+1)\rightarrow$
questions.answer: $|x|/(n+1)\rightarrow0<1$ for all $x\Rightarrow R=\infty$.
